cards.a: Latin - Croatia, Montenegro, Serbia Shared Latin Letters
cards.note:
• Countries: Croatia, Montenegro, Serbia
  • Info: The lowercase đ is reasonably rare because most words containing đ have it as the first letter, or are in all caps on shop signs, so the upper case letter is often used, however the lower case can be seen occasionally. Much more likely to be found in Croatia just due to there being more coverage there.
  • Warnings: đ is the lower case form of Đ (D with stroke), not to be confused with the almost identical Đ (Eth) which is found in Bosnian, Serbian & Croatian.
• Countries: Czechia

cards.a: Latin - Faroe Islands, Iceland Shared Latin Letters
cards.note:
• Countries: Faroe Islands, Iceland
  • Info: ð can also be found in Sami regions.
  • Warnings: ð is the lower case form of Đ (Eth), not to be confused with the almost identical Đ (D with stroke) which can be found in some other languages such as Bosnian, Serbian & Croatian.

• Countries: France
  • Info: While the Œ ligature, unique to French, is found in other French speaking countries, in practice it will usually be expanded to OE, so if you see it on signage within Europe, you are far more likely to be in France.

• Countries: Portugal, Estonia
  • Warnings: Õõ can also be found in Sami regions (Skolt)

• Countries: Romania
  • Warnings: Be careful not to confuse Șș with the Turkish Şş. Ââ can also be found in Sami regions.
• Countries: Slovakia

• Countries: Spain
  • Info: Ññ (sometimes written as N with a ¯ [Macron diactiric] above instead), found in Spanish, is effectively unique to Spain (within Europe), though possible rarely in France and perhaps elsewhere via minor languages such as Basque.

• Countries: Turkiye
  • Info: İi, while a distinct letter, can obviously be confused with other forms of i. It's quite recognisable on signs as Turkish though, so it's been included.
  • Warnings: Be careful not to confuse Şş with the Romanian Șș. Ğğ can also be found in Sami regions.

• Countries: Wales
  • Unique Letters: Ŵŵ Ŷŷ
  • Info: Both quite rare, but Ŵŵ more so. Welsh itself is fairly uncommon in streetview.
